Name: Pilgrim Beart FIET
How_knew_David: Cambridge technology innovator
Tribute: David achieved an extraordinary amount in a short life, and was a lovely person too. Here's how he's changed my life, in “numbers, not adjectives": In 2008, an early proof of SEWTHA was a cold splash of reality, prompting me to pivot the smart home startup I'd co-founded, AlertMe, to focus on home energy management.  AlertMe became Hive, which today serves around three million UK homes and in 2025 claimed 6.2 TWh gas avoided and ~1.5 MtCO₂ avoided. David was a true polymath, with impact spanning education, startups, assistive technologies, and UK energy policy. I miss him and in this new era of LLMs, descendants of the statistical inference and information-theoretic ideas to which he contributed so much, I wonder what piquant observations he might make about their "truth per joule"?

Name: Ben Coppin
Tribute: David's book (SEWTHA) was a game-changer. It was so clear and objective, in contrast with most other materials available at the time on the subject of climate change. I was working at a startup, looking at how AI could be used to help consumers measure and reduce their energy consumption, and David was very generous with his time and his feedback. I still use quotes from his book and refer people to it today, as there really hasn't been a more clearly reasoned work on the subject since.

Name: Dr Justin Hayward
Tribute: Both energy/materials books and ITILA. I wrote a generalised game show tribute to David and his Bayesian proof in my own book. His support of the Bayes inference approach inspired me.

Name: Dr Leopold Parts
How_knew_David: David was my University Supervisor during my Ph.D
Tribute: I interacted with David's inference research group at the Cavendish often, and personally with him a few times. Directly, the talks I gave to the group were deconstructed to get at the core of the problem, looking for clarity in both the setup and the solution, which forced me to level up my work. Indirectly, the "everything is connected" and "everything is quantifiable" philosophies expanded in ITILA and SEWTHA exposed a diversity- and reality-grounded worldview that I grew to subscribe to, as well as a very human whimsy that I learned to cherish in everyone.

Name: Dr Weiwei Sun
How_knew_David: University of Cambridge
Tribute: ITILA has changed my understanding of machine learning.

Name: Professor Sir Harshad Bhadeshia, FRS, FREng
How_knew_David: Darwin College
Tribute:
Following a casual conversation during lunch at Darwin College, David and I developed a major collaboration. My area of expertise is physical metallurgy, and I was interested in understanding and applying neural network methods to model the relationship between the chemical composition, structure and complex properties in steels. These properties, such as toughness and fatigue, can be measured routinely and used in the safe design of engineering structures. They are, however, so complex that there is no adequate theory that can predict them, except in all but the simplest of cases that are not technologically relevant. Given our vastly different backgrounds, it took time and patience to establish a common language between us, but the collaboration turned out to be productive,
leading to a series of 14 joint papers, whose significance I described in my review paper of 1999.

David helped in particular to implement his Bayesian and evidence frameworks, which were seminal in avoiding the overfitting problem, leading to some remarkable quantitative predictions even when faced with myriads of input variables. He introduced the concept of modelling uncertainty, which is independent of the noise that is experienced when an experiment is repeated. This made the models safe to apply because it helped identify domains within the input space where knowledge is sparse or where estimates are made far beyond the known parameters. When combined with thermodynamics and kinetic theory, the work enabled, and continues to enable, the creation of novel alloys to be dramatically accelerated through a rational, evidence-based process that made maximum use of information and thereby reduced the resources needed for the task. Examples include fire-resistant steel, alloys for futuristic power plants and alloys used in the cast condition.

These successes led to David’s ‘bigback’ algorithm being adopted in materials research in many parts of the world; more generally, the strategy of combining mechanistic or thermodynamic modelling with informatic, ‘data-mining’ approaches has been very widely copied since then as a way to speed up materials discovery.

Name: Dr. Salvatore Scellato, PhD
How_knew_David: Ex Director of Engineering at Google DeepMind, currently still working in Machine Learning
Tribute:
As a young and newly minted PhD student at the university of Cambridge I attended one of his lectures on sustainable energy. It was so inspiring, so clear, and so thought-provoking. I only then realised it was the same person how had written ITILA, the book I was studying on to better understand Machine Learning. 

Such an intellectual giant, such an inspiration.

Name: Eiko Yoneki
How_knew_David: University of Cambridge
Tribute: His pioneer work on Bayesian inference to neural networks really gave a new direction of work to me.

Name: Michael Liebreich
How_knew_David: Host, Cleaning Up
Tribute: Renewable Energy Without The Hot Air was a breath of fresh air in the energy culture wars. It wasn't that it told me things I didn't know - indeed in some areas David profoundly underestimated the likelihood of technological and economic advances. But it demonstrated how we need to build energy policy on a foundation of science and engineering, not of politics, hope and self-delusion.

Name: Jorge Tendeiro
Tribute:
I am deeply humbled and eternally grateful for a chance to explain how Professor David MacKay saved my life.

Through a small, free, open-source app called Dasher, this remarkable man restored my voice, independence, and will to live. Dasher lets people with severe motor impairments write fluently using continuous gestures via mouse, joystick, head tracker, eyegaze, or any remaining movement. I’ve tried many other communication systems for the severely disabled, and yet, this obscure, exceptionally brilliant project, even today, has no  rivals in its simplicity, speed, or gentle usability—nothing out there is even in the same ballpark.

Diagnosed with Motor Neuron Disease in 2005, by 2009 paralysis had stolen my ability to type, write by hand, or speak clearly. Existing communication aids felt torturously slow and draining, each word an exhausting fight.

Then, in what still feels like providence, I found Dasher on the Inference Group site. Within a day, I wrote near my former speed. Within a week, I texted, emailed, and spoke via text-to-speech as naturally as before. This unassuming tool reopened my world.
Dasher gave me purpose each morning. I pursued online Philosophy studies, earned a writing degree and diplomas, and built a thriving online business. Above all, it kept me connected to family, friends, deep conversations, and the simple joy of being heard. These connections gave me the will and motivation for a life worth fighting for.
Without Dasher, despair might have won earlier, through my own choice or the disease’s relentless advance. Instead, it let me live as if I was going to live: dreaming, planning, and creating.

Twenty years into MND, I still write every word—including this tribute—with the tool he created. Professor MacKay’s legacy lives in the dignity and hope he quietly returned to me and countless others. I hope some students or professionals continue developing and improving this miraculous app for current and future generations. Who knows, it may be someone you know who will rediscover the will to live through using Dasher.
In closing, Professor MacKay didn’t just make software...he built a bridge back to my life.

Name: Dr. Soren Brage, PhD
How_knew_David: MRC Epidemiology Unit, University of Cambridge.
Tribute: We worked together on inference of heart rate from noisy sensor data collected by wearables. We published the paper in 2008 with his PhD student Oliver Stegle as first author and we still use the method today in large population studies; this timelessness of the science is a testament to the academic values that David - and the academics around him - aspired to. As wearables are becoming more and more common in the general population, and as the pressure continues to build to produce cheaper and cheaper consumer products, I suspect the method will only become more relevant in the future if we are to gain true health insights from such data, a legacy of David's work that I am proud and humbled to share with him.

Name: Mick Donegan, PhD, MBE
How_knew_David: At the time I met David I was Deputy Director of the ACE Centre, Oxford
Tribute: I was introduced to David by ‘The Gatsby Foundation’ who, in the early 2000's, introduced us to each other and funded a joint project to optimise the use of Dasher for Eye Gaze. We called it 'The DECO (Dasher for Eye Control Optimisation) Project’. The outcome was highly successful in both raising awareness of Dasher and increasing the number of eye gaze users of the software. A talk I gave on behalf of both David and myself at the “ISAAC (International Society for Augmentative and Alternative Communication) Conference” in Brazil in 2006 was voted the best presentation of the conference. I was also fortunate enough to collaborate with David during the EU-funded COGAIN (Communication by Gaze Interaction) Project (2004- 2009) that involved Universities and Assistive Technology Centres from across Europe. I feel privileged to have known him and even more privileged to have had the opportunity to work alongside him.

Name: Prof. Stephen Roberts, FREng
How_knew_David: University of Oxford
Tribute: David’s work on Bayesian methods in machine learning fundamentally reshaped my sense of what was possible. Through his ideas, uncertainty stopped being a nuisance to be engineered away and became a first-class citizen, something to be understood and respected. Our conversations, ranging from the deep connections between uncertainty and energy–entropy tradeoffs to the hard, practical question of how to scale Bayesian methods to real-world problems, were endlessly fascinating. He had a rare ability to move effortlessly between principle and practice, showing that mathematical rigour, efficient computation and real-world application need not be at odds. What made David truly exceptional was not only the depth of his insight, but the generosity and clarity with which he shared it. He was never short of a wonderful analogy that could illuminate a difficult concept and he constantly encouraged thinking beyond accepted limits. In doing so, he helped extend the boundaries of the art of the possible, inspiring those around him to aim higher and think more boldly. His influence endures not just in methods and models, but in the way many of us now think about probabilistic learning, uncertainty and the creative reach of machine learning.

Name: John J Hopfield
Tribute:
David Mackay was one of the most selfless physicists I have known. 

He was a lecturer in my course at Caltech in the 90's. He wrote out problem sets and answers for the course. He wrote instructive books on energy and physics. Not only were the books useful, but he gave them away whenever possible. He understood the physics of every device he approached.

Finding himself with incurable cancer and in Addenbrooke's, he developed a public blog aiming at improving conditions in the ward, even with humor.  

A close associate who also completed his Ph.D with me at Caltech, was Sanjoy Mahajan, who is now on the Physics faculty at the University of Lund. I attach a photograph of me and David at the Royal Society in August 2012. 

Here is a quote I made in his original obituary:
" John Hopfield has described as follows the positive impact David made at Caltech: 

No description of David at Caltech would be complete without mentioning the effect of his clarity of thought and exposition on those around him. He was a concise and constructive critic of the research of others, a joyful participant in wide-ranging scholarly debate." 

A truly admirable man, worthy of great posthumous remembrance.

Thanks for your taking on this task, from the many whose lives he enhanced.

Name: Prof. Franck Tancret
How_knew_David: Collaborator at the University of Cambridge 1998-2000
Tribute: I met David MacKay on a few occasions while I was a postdoc in Cambridge between 1998 and 2000, working on alloy design in the Department of Materials Science and Metallurgy with Harry Bhadeshia, who was a close friend of David. They had met as fellows at Darwin College, where the magic of Cambridge colleges operated exactly as it is meant to: through social events, people from very different academic domains meet, talk, get along, and sometimes imagine improbable collaborations. In this case, it was the application of learning algorithms to metallurgy, as tools for alloy design. What sounded like a rather bizarre idea at the time would become, in the following decades, one of the most active fields in materials science. Today, "machine learning" is present in most materials science studies worldwide. Back then, I was simply curious about these methods and about how they could be applied to my own field. Reading David's papers, discussing with him and using his codes, Bayesian learning progressively became as natural to me as using an optical microscope or a microhardness tester. It was only later, when I started presenting my work to the wider materials community, that I realised —through people’s reactions— that David and Harry had in fact opened up a completely new field of research. At the time, this sometimes meant being perceived as a curious beast or an extraterrestrial! I eventually lost contact with David, but all my career I continued to work on alloy design using these methods, trying to associate them to other tools. I followed with interest the rapid rise of "artificial intelligence", largely driven by deep learning. Yet, in retrospect, and considering the typically small, noisy, and scattered datasets encountered in metallurgy, I find David’s work on information theory and Bayesian learning and inference more inspiring than ever. As recently as January 2026, I had the opportunity to cite ITILA in a seminar entitled "AI in materials science: small data versus big data", highlighting the enduring relevance of David’s approach in an "AI world" obsessed with trillions of tokens and parameters. As an "ultimate" point, this also resonates with another of David’s messages: the importance of sobriety in both the treatment of data and the use of energy.

Name: Sean Eddy
How_knew_David: First met him at MRC-LMB in the 1990's. Wrote a short paper with him. Played ultimate frisbee with him on some Sundays!
Tribute:
I first met David when I joined the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge in 1992 as a postdoc in computational biology. One of my postdoc mentors was Richard Durbin, Richard was working closely with Graeme Mitchison, and both Richard and Graeme had been talking to David about new inference problems arising in genome sequence analysis. David would come up to the LMB to join our computational biology discussion group.

David immediately saw every problem as a Bayesian inference problem. What's the data, what's the model, what are the parameters of interest, what are the nuisance parameters, what do you want to infer from the data; write down the probability of everything, turn the crank.  The clarity and swaggering confidence of David's approach was an epiphany. Suddenly the genomics problems I had been struggling to think about were illuminated in a common framework that always made sense and almost always worked. I became a convert and an acolyte to the gospel David preached to us. Sometime around when I first met him I asked him what the J.C. stood for in David J.C. MacKay and he said "Jesus Christ" with a straight face and to this day I'm not sure if he was joking.

I teach Bayesian statistical inference to undergraduate quantitative biologists at Harvard now, and every year there's the part where I stop to tell them about David.

Name: Iain McLean FBA FRSE
How_knew_David: Co-author and avid reader of SEWTHA
Tribute:
I may have been David’s most remote co-author. We were brought together by our third co-author, Roger Sewell, to write a paper on probabilistic voting schemes that bypass Arrow’s paradox (If you know why this matters, you know).The paper is 'Probabilistic electoral methods, representative probability, and maximum entropy' "Voting Matters" 2009. Though very remote from David’s main work, the paper has the unmistakable MacKay light touch and pedagogical deftness. The hard maths is in an appendix, replaced in the main text by A Tutorial Exposition. This is exactly the approach of David’s magnum opus  SEWTHA, which radically changed my lifestyle..

SEWTHA remains a pedagogic marvel. I keep it by my bed and reread p.24 constantly, to make sure I understand the difference between units of energy and units of power: a lesson the world and the media need as much now as they did then. It has completely changed my driving and house-heating habits (though on the latter I am not nearly as extreme as he was). Like many others I am fascinated by which of David’s predictions have done well and which have done badly. Solar and wind energy in the UK have expanded far quicker, and coal has disappeared far quicker, than he anticipated; on the other hand tidal generation, where the physics is rock-solid, has failed to go anywhere. Of course, some of the changes that have made David’s book out of date may be due to David himself and to Ed Miliband, who made the inspired appointment of David to be chief scientist at the energy department in 2009.

Name: Neil Lawrence
How_knew_David: Student who attended inference group, later colleague, reader of books, I would hope friend!
Tribute:
David didn't just change my life, he continues to change, modify and mould. Not just through his works, actions and ideas, but also through his relationships. David didn't only inspire individuals, he inspired communities. 

Having David as a shared acquaintance is a ticket to a more sophisticated conversation. You simply have to ask, "how would David have approached this". While we cannot fully replicate what he would have done, we can aspire to approach it. We can remember together the precision his thinking would have brought to the problem. And as we debate the approaches we find that David still bonds us today. Whenever we are together we have more of David there than when we are alone. As he was fond of saying, everything is connected, and we are more connected because of him.

Name: Dr Alan Lawrence MA PhD
How_knew_David: Postdoc supervisor in the Inference Group
Tribute: I've had the pleasure of working with a few great minds such as David in various roles. All have seen further than I, but David stands out in a couple of ways. Firstly, these minds vary in how much patience they had with idiots like me. David seemed to have infinite patience. Secondly, in their efforts to apply their knowledge in helping others. David stood out in how he tried to both solve humanity's greatest problems (in SEWTHA) and to help those in greatest need (e.g. the Dasher project). He is sorely missed.

Name: Professor Michelle Povinelli, PhD
How_knew_David: Churchill Scholar and MPhil Student, 1997-8, Inference Group
Tribute: David was a creative and original scholar who took real intellectual risks. He did not stick to a narrow field, nor try and "maximize his output" along a narrow technical trajectory. Instead, decided to take on one of the biggest problems of our age, how to make human energy usage sustainable, and attacked it head on, first through his book, and then through his work with government. His boldness is inspirational.

Name: David Duvenaud
How_knew_David: Had dinner with him once, know most of his students well.
Tribute:
I only spoke at length with David Mackay a couple of times, but he's loomed large in my life.  Both as the advisor to many of my friends and colleagues, but even more importantly to me, as a figure to emulate.

I have many colleagues and mentors who have excellent judgement in their areas of expertise, but what set David apart was his ability to weigh sensibly in on apparently any subject, without making a fool of himself.  I think in doing so he set the standard for how brilliant and accomplished people can and should carry themselves.

He didn't seek politics or drama for its own sake, but he equally wasn't cowed by the apparent expertise of others or the standard academic polite practice of leaving unfamiliar matters to those with the corresponding credentials.  By doing this, he provided a civilizational "defense in depth" against important fields becoming politically captured.

I also learned a lot from his blog detailing his dying of cancer.  I've attempted to emulate his amazing attitude when facing similar struggles.

Name: Ruediger Urbanke
How_knew_David: Colleague working in information theory and in particular coding.
Tribute: David was a wonderful colleague who brought a breath of fresh air into the information theory and coding community. He had an extremely broad background, with interests spanning statistical physics, machine learning, information theory, and sustainable energy. This allowed him to see things in a new light and to connect dots that had not been connected before. He was less interested in the epsilons and deltas—where our community often gets stuck—than in the broad and important ideas. He was always fun to talk to, with strong opinions and a great sense of humour. In one of our last conversations, when—who knows how—we got talking about his strong opinions, he pointed out that in his family his brother was the one who was considered opinionated! But most of all, any opinion was, to him, something to be tested by the scientific method. He is dearly missed, as a visionary, a great scientist, and as a friend.

Name: Professor Lewis Barlow
How_knew_David: Read his book through a friend.
Tribute:
David MacKay’s work runs through almost everything I do professionally. I reference him in nearly all of my training, not out of habit, but because his way of thinking about energy and climate change remains foundational.

What resonated most strongly with me—and still does—is his insistence on numbers, not adjectives. David showed that credibility in climate and energy discussions comes from doing the maths, being explicit about assumptions, and being honest about trade-offs. That approach has shaped how I communicate about decarbonisation: grounded, quantitative, and resistant to slogans, greenwashing, or what David himself would have called “bullshit”.

Through Sustainable Energy – Without the Hot Air, and through his lectures and videos, David also articulated something deeper than analysis alone: a clear motivation for why sustainable energy matters, without moralising or oversimplifying. He treated the audience with respect, trusted them with complexity, and showed that rigorous thinking is not a barrier to action but a prerequisite for it.

I am proud to help keep David’s legacy alive through my training and professional work. I regularly use his material—particularly his last interview with Mark Lynas —because it still cuts through in a way few others do. Not only because his legacy needs preserving for its own sake, but because the discipline, clarity, and intellectual honesty he championed are still urgently needed.

Name: Mark Crouch
How_knew_David: Read his book and inspired by his work
Tribute:
David's work set me on the path to working on sustainable energy and decarbonisation. Reading SEWTHA inspired me to start thinking about climate change mitigation as a whole system problem, and based on solid evidence and analysis. After reading his brilliant book, I decided to take a sabbatical and study the Sustainable Energy Futures MSc at Imperial College. It was a highlight of my course to get David (then CSA at DECC) to speak as keynote at our MSc conference, where all the students presented our research projects. 

Following the course I took a career pivot to work on decarbonisation, which I have been doing for the last 15 years. Many years later in my current job, we have been working in emerging economies globally, helping governments to use the Mackay Carbon Calculator to inform their decarbonation and energy policies, and also working closely with DESNZ. David was a huge influence on me and countless others in applying ourselves to the energy and climate challenge. RIP!

Name: Peter Kydd CEng FICE
How_knew_David: He was part of the client team at DECC
Tribute: I first read the on-line version of SEWTHA around 2008/9 and was amazed how one book could cover the essence of our energy system so effectively.  After David was appointed as CSA to DECC a year later, I was lucky enough to attend a lecture with him on Severn Tidal Power (I had led the consulting team advising DECC)   He turned up with his trademark briefcase and pulled out a printed copy of SEWTHA and handed it to me.  I use it to this day.

Name: Marc Deisenroth
Tribute: David was a great inspiration to me as a PhD student. His wealth of knowledge was incredible, and the way he could explain and make connections were remarkable. He once told me (half jokingly) that he was shifting his research focus every 5 years or so because he believed he'd made enough of a contribution to the field that others can start picking up and solve the really hard problems. When he was working on SEWTHA, he was the first one who confronted me with some actual numbers on how we could get rid of fossil fuels and what kind of a huge task this will be; but it was possible. It was a great to see him looking at the very hard, societal problems with an approach of passion and pragmatism. In a sense this has planted a seed me and probably influenced my future direction.

Name: Simon Richards MSc MEI
How_knew_David: Read his book
Tribute: I read SEWTHA whilst a head of sustainability at a FTSE250 firm (a role that I requested be established having held a succession of senior commercial roles there). The book made me want to study energy at postgrad level. I managed a few years later to fund that full time study, and one of my Professor's often quoted David (whom he had met). I read SEWTHA again, and sometimes cited it in my assignments. I decided to name Sir David in the dedication to my dissertation, and the logic in SEWTHA helped me achieve a Distinction. When I look at the framed degree certificate, and write my post nominal MSc I often think of David and quietly thank him.

Name: George Cybenko, Dorothy and Walter Gramm Professor of Engineering, Dartmouth College
How_knew_David: Read ITILA
Tribute:
I didn't know David personally but was a great admirer of his work.
ITILA is an enduring masterpiece to which I often refer my graduate students.  He was a
giant and is being sorely missed.

Name: Mark Lynas
How_knew_David: Friend and colleague
Tribute: I still miss David, and think about him often. The world is changing rapidly, on energy and climate and in many other ways, and I would have loved to still be able to hear David's insight and wisdom. People occasionally email me and ask about updating SEWTHA - I'm not sure why these queries come to me; perhaps because David and I did a roadshow many years ago showcasing his Calculator to live audiences. But I think SWETHA is of its time and still somehow timeless... having said that I'm perhaps more optimistic about the rapidity of the energy transition than I was when David wrote this book. The physics haven't changed, but the economics certainly have. I wish he were still around to see it.

Name: Adrian Critchlow Founder of Australian Solar Group (co-founder of Booking.com)
How_knew_David: Met in Cambridge and read his excellent book
Tribute: David was amazingly open and helpful when we met and ultimately he inspired me to build utility scale solar farms in Australia, so hopefully he is looking down with a smile!

Name: Geoffrey Hinton CC FRS, Nobel Laureate
How_knew_David: personal friend and professional colleague
Tribute:
I first met David when I was presenting a poster at NIPS. He asked several questions about the work that made me think "why didn't I think of that?" After about 5 minutes I offered him a postdoc position in Toronto but he was already planning to take up a fellowship in Cambridge.  

David was incredibly talented but also very kind. He stayed with me quite often in Toronto when he was working with Radford Neal and he always brought Wallace and Grommet presents for my children who loved him dearly.

David immediately understood and appreciated the "bits-back" argument that was an important intuitive crutch when developing variational inference and learning.  The argument   asserts that the receiver can recover the random bits used by the sender to stochastically pick one of several possible codes for the same message. This means that those random bits can be used to transmit some other message, so the true cost of sending the message is the expected number of bits needed to send the selected code MINUS the entropy of the distribution from which it is selected. It has exactly the form of a free energy.  

In addition to being a brilliant scientist, David had a strong sense of social responsibility and he really made a difference with his SEWTHA book and his subsequent role as the government's chief scientific adviser on energy and climate change.  When he took up his government role, David asked me if I had any advice for him.  I advised him to wear long trousers. 

I was staying at David's house a few days before he took up his government position and at 6.05am the phone went. It was his new boss, the permanent secretary, calling to reprimand him.  The day before, he had given an interview to the BBC in which the journalist told him that someone had said that the UK would run out of energy in 2017 (or thereabouts). David said that was not right. The journalist then asked if it was possible. David, being a true Bayesian, said anything was possible. The lead story on the BBC science website the next morning at 6.00am was that the new scientific advisor said we might run out of energy in 2017. One of David's most endearing characteristics was his unwavering intellectual honesty which made it hard for him to see how people might twist his words. 

David's death was a huge loss for the scientific community and it is very sad that he did not live to see the eventual success of neural networks which had always fascinated him.

Name: Adrian Sharman
Tribute: I found "Sustainable energy - without the hot air" in a second-hand bookshop and thought it sounded interesting. It started me on the path of doing much more research about sustainability that ended up completely changing my views on how society needs to be organised. SEWTHA is one of those books (along with Prosperity without growth by Tim Jackson) that I urge people to read if they want to understand where we are and what we need to do.

Name: Matthias Seeger
Tribute:
David is one of my science all-time-heroes, his writings and argumentation formed my thinking (I recall vividly him and Radford Neal taking apart frequentist arguments during a Royal Society of Edinburgh meeting). But even more (how is this possible?) than his putting ML and neural networks on a solid Bayesian foundation, I was impressed and guided by his work on Sustainable Energy.

Many many people (including myself) talk, but David
walks the walk. It is such a profound loss, and I often wonder what David's contributions would be to AI or Climate Change policy today, or whatever his great mind would have identified to address as the next big problem to bring clarity and action to.

Name: Jose Miguel Hernandez Lobato
How_knew_David: Read his book, attended his lectures and talks. Built on his research on the Laplace approximation to neural networks.
Tribute: David's book "Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms" was my first serious introduction to Machine Learning when I was a PhD student. I loved it! David's work on the Laplace approximation to neural networks had a big influence in my own research.

Name: Tiago Peixoto
How_knew_David: Read his books.
Tribute: ITILA is probably the best textbook ever written.

Name: Jonathan Rougier
Tribute: David, whom I did not know well, continues to influence me through his books, not just the material, but also the playful and engaging style, which I try to emulate, and the flashes of brilliance, which I never could.

Name: Roland F. Schwarz, PhD
How_knew_David: we collaborated on DNA storage
Tribute: I only met David a few times during my work at EBI on the DNA storage project, but he left a lasting impression on me through both his brilliance and his kindness.

Name: Max Welling
How_knew_David: We knew each other and of each others work, but never worked together.
Tribute: David's work introduced me to the beauty of Bayesian ML. Moreover, I learned about MCMC and BP from his work. Of course I bought his book ITILA and I share his passion to act on climate change. (And I tried Dasher but failed to increase my typing speed..) He was a hero of a time where beautiful ideas still made a difference and AI was not just about scaling laws...

Name: Prof. Helmut Grubmüller
How_knew_David: We met for just a few hours discussion on occasion of David's visit here in Goettingen for his lecture  within the scope of the Goettingen Autumn Literature Festival.
Tribute:
I vividly recall David's visit to Goettingen, where we discussed with great pleasure and enthusiasm the physics of molecular motors. It was immediately clear
that David and myself were speaking a very similar physics language; combined with his insatisfyable curiosity, that was a very memorable day.
I should also mention that the reason we invited David to Goettingen was his visionary book on sustainable energy which, looking back from today's perspective,
got everything just right. Still, I wish politicians and decision-makers read this book, which, if really understood and applied, would change the world for better.

Name: Stephan ten Brink
How_knew_David: the first time I met David was at my poster at the Turbo Symposium in Brest, France, Sept. 2000
Tribute: He was very quick in capturing the "core" of novel technical approaches, and was benevolently sharing ideas on further improvements. During only 10min of discussion at my poster on convergence of iterative decoding (Turbo Symposium, Brest, France, Sept. 2000) I got inspiration and material for doing research for the next 3 years...

Name: Brendan Frey
How_knew_David: Friend and colleague
Tribute: David and I were good friends and collaborated on machine learning and digital communications. I liked that he was inspiring, direct and optimistic, both in our personal lives and in our research. We had a lot of great debates across a wide range of topics, from neural networks to how dangerous it really is to go over Niagara falls in a barrel. I miss him.

Name: Roger Sewell
How_knew_David: Family friend
Tribute: David introduced me to the practical use of Bayes - from which I never looked back. He was also the best-behaved teenager I have ever encountered.

Name: Philip Sargent
How_knew_David: From Cambridge, and worked together at DECC
Tribute:
Although I didn't meet him at the event, David came to the inaugural meeting of our Cambridge Energy Forum
in January 2005; where Sir David King gave the talk. David later said that this had renewed his determination to
do something in energy which resulted in "Sustainable Energy without the Hot Air". David came to a few of
the Forum meetings after that.

A software engineer, Adrian Wrigley, attending the forum meetings had an idea about tidal energy and I put him in
touch with David and the three of us formed a company, wrote a patent, and David applied for grant money to
support Adrian to continue the research. This was all in the first half of 2007. What happened next was typical
when you work with David. He had another think, and had some further inspiration (tidal energy has some tricky physics),
and he came to see that maybe we had had it all backwards: that a resonator at tidal frequencies was actually exactly
the wrong thing to do. At the same time we all determined that the experimental data we had been using for seabed
bottom friction was probably completely bogus: which killed the idea, resonant or not. None of us had any difficulty with
that conclusion but in retrospect I realise that this is not common human behaviour. Some of David's analysis
of the tidal physics remains unpublished and we should probably do something about that.

In 2012 the startup technology company I had been working at was running out of steam and a colleague of the Forum,
Tim, who knew David well, rang me to say that after a year or so as Chief Scientific Advisor to DECC, David still hadn't
managed to fill his team of engineers and would I be interested, or did I know anybody. Civil service processes are
not fast and it was 7 months later in October 2012 that I began work as a G7 engineer in David's immediate team of a dozen
engineers.

Working in DECC was great: I was surrounded by clever people, working on important issues in renewable heat and bioenergy.
The team's unfortunate habit of showing the rest of the department that favourite policy proposals often didn't add up
did not endear us to career civil servants, and David shouldered the responsibility of supporting us without a thought.
Despite what you might expect from an extraordinarily capable physicist, David had absolutely no difficulty in seeing
that what the department needed most urgently was engineers. His achievement in getting a substantial, if small,
central engineering team in place is one of his most important - but unsung - achievements. (That team is still there,
now in the Dept. of Energy Security and Net Zero.)

We were a rather informal group at DECC, encouraged by David. I remember our Christmas parties held in 3 Whitehall Place
in the late afternoon, where fancy dress was the rule and David would participate in pairwise space-hopper races
in a 20m course between the desks. Happy days.

Name: Matthew D. Hoffman
How_knew_David: Fan of his work and collaborator with some of his students
Tribute: Sadly I never had the privilege of meeting him, but Professor MacKay taught me quite a bit through his papers, his book on information theory, and, by no means least, his brilliant (and brilliantly trained) students.

Name: Miguel Angel Yescas Gonzalez
How_knew_David: I met David at Darwin College during my time in Cambridge (1998-2001)
Tribute:
From the beginning, it was clear that David was a man of deep convictions and genuine respect for others. His intellect was remarkable. I had the privilege of using his ITILA to build neural network models in materials science, and each time I did, I was reminded of his brilliance and clarity of thought.
David was exceptionally gifted, an ascending star in every sense. His legacy is enormous, not only through his scientific contributions but also through the integrity and kindness he showed to those around him. If he were still with us today, I have no doubt he would have reached even greater achievements.

Name: Pr. Eric Moulines
How_knew_David: colleague working in the same field
Tribute: David  was a very brilliant mind. We shared many common interests: Bayesian networks, inference in hierarchical models, and also a desire to produce research that would not be entirely ‘sterile’ but would lead to real applications. I only realized too late the importance of his fight for a decarbonized world. I’m looking into what I can do.

Name: Dr Richard Kembleton
How_knew_David: Student, read his books, had some personal interactions about fusion energy
Tribute: I attended David's lectures on information theory, and applied his methods during my PhD. Learning about inference from him changed the way I think about data and machine learning, and I still refer to ITILA and SEWTHA when I want to reduce ideas about information or energy down to bare essentials. We invited him to visit UKAEA during early drafting of SEWTHA and appreciated his openness and curiousity.

Name: Hiroaki Minato
Tribute: David and his writings inspired me to contribute in the energy domain as a statistician.

Name: Phil Withers (Regius Prof. of Materials)
How_knew_David: Friend and colleague
Tribute: Meeting David (thanks to Harry Bhadeshia and Darwin college (and to a lesser extent the films of Charlie Chan (?) which I think Harry and David shared an interest in)) was a turning point for me - we started to work on applying neural networks to materials science with his help a long time before AI was in vogue.  Furthermore I was inspired by the way David was brave enough to apply the physics analytical approach to a wide range of topics outside his comfort zone  and then to follow it through, as evidenced by SEWTHA becoming Chief Scientific Advisor to the UK Department of Energy and Climate Change (DECC). I valued his warmth and guidance in all things Bayesian.  He is really missed.

Name: Prof. Andreas Herz
Tribute: David loved this world and deeply believed that scientific reasoning can make it a better place.

Name: Nick Goldman
How_knew_David: I knew David through the Cambridge 'probability community' and then as thesis committee member for some of my students and advisor on scientific projects and grants
Tribute:
Many people will have more to say about David's brilliance in his own fields. My experience of him was more when he gave me and my colleagues and students the benefit of his probability and coding insights into problems in *our* specialisms. He was one of the very few people who could rapidly understand new problems and cut to the heart of them with fresh insights and actionable plans. Unlike some others with this skill, he achieved this in a way that made it feel like a valuable collaboration that you were being entrusted to proceed with, and not a trivial gift from a genius to a mere mortal. Which may have been what it was, but not what anyone wants to hear.

By acting in this way with me and my students in particular, I always felt he made a much greater contribution. We felt our research was interesting and important, and we always left with new ideas of where we could go next with it. The inspiration was arguably just as important as the actual advice.

Name: Prof Adrian Weller MBE
How_knew_David: I read his books and reached out to talk. He kindly and patiently took time. I was thrilled and deeply honoured to be the first David MacKay Newton Research Fellow at Darwin College. David continues to be a huge inspiration to me and many others.
Tribute: I loved his books, I loved how he thought and his teaching style, and I loved that he put great efforts into trying to change the world for the better. I also hugely admire his amazing endurance and transparency in dealing with his health issues at the end.

Name: Michael Betancourt, PhD
How_knew_David: Read his book
Tribute:
At the beginning of my PhD I was assigned a difficult data analysis project; in preparation I started looking for useful data analysis references.  One of my undergrad classmates recommended “Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms” and, as so many others have experienced, I was immediately fascinated.  David’s writing was lucid yet playful; I laughed as much as I learned, and I learned _a lot_.

I vividly remember the broken detector example in Chapter 3 demonstrating the natural interplay between statistics and science, and how it contrasted with the disconnect between statistics and science that had plagued so much of my academic course work.  My ongoing work on methodology that bridges statistics and science can all be traced back to that example.

His introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo was my first real experience with Markov chain Monte Carlo.  It inspired not only a hand-coded implementation for my thesis analysis, but also a theoretical research program that lead to a deeper understanding of the method.  Those insights then made direct improvements to Stan, and from there many other probabilistic programming tools.  

A common theme in that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo research has been understanding the behavior of probability distributions and probabilistic computation in high-dimensions.  Here, too, David’s writing provided critical understanding.  The way I conceptualize and communicate these high-dimensional behaviors all derives from his discussion of typical sets and concentration of measure.

I had the privilege of meeting David in person a few times, and he never ceased to be kind and entertaining.  A few months before he passed we both attended a small workshop, which gave me the opportunity to thank him for his work and its influence on my own.  After ten years I am grateful to have the opportunity to continue sharing his work, and see how it continues to help and inspire others.

Name: Andrew Childs
How_knew_David: Student in his course and collaborator on "Exact sampling from non-attractive distributions using summary states"
Tribute: I learned information theory from David during a term spent as an exchange student at Cambridge in early 2000. His lectures and his book were both incredibly inspiring. David's teaching was a model of clarity, and he cared deeply both about the subject and about bringing it to a wider audience. I also had the amazing opportunity to do a small research project with David (and another Caltech exchange student) during that term. Working with David was wonderful. He gave us a framework and the freedom to explore on our own, and at the same time wasn't above getting into the weeds. I miss interacting with him, and I'm grateful for his impact on my career.

Name: David Barber
Tribute: I first came across David's work in the early 1990s as I tried to understand Machine Learning, generalisation and overfitting. Amongst the different schools of thought, David's Bayesian approach stood out for me as a principled way to think about parameter fitting and model selection. His papers (and his PhD thesis) brought clarity to an otherwise confusing scene and he was gifted with the ability to explain his ideas simply and widely. David was a towering figure in our community and his influence was enormous, even after he later focussed his attention outside of Machine Learning.  He achieved so much in his scientific life, in Machine Learning, Information Theory and Energy -- an intellectual mentor to many. He pioneered free textbooks in Machine Learning, championed environmental causes,  donating money also to the defence of Sally Clark.  At his heart, David was a man of principle who passionately supported the causes he believed in. The world is poorer without him, but enriched by his lasting impact.

Name: Sylvain Condamin, PhD.
How_knew_David: Student of his, read his book.
Tribute: I met David as an exchange student, and I am very thankful for his warm welcome in the Inference group. He had the rare ability to build bridges between different fields of research, as well as a deep sense of the greater good. SEWTHA was a masterful work, one of the best books made to enlighten the public debate.

Name: Seb Wills
How_knew_David: student and postdoc of his, and personal friend
Tribute:
David's undergrad course on information theory and neural networks blew my mind wide open. Each lecture was a beautifully crafted story, Feynman-esque, with lecture notes that were the early drafts of ITILA. He was a teacher eager to take every opportunity to improve the clarity of insight he was offering, constantly seeking feedback. David's openness and inclusivity extended naturally to undergraduates. An email expressing an interest in a PhD in the Inference Group brought, by return, an invitation to chat over dinner at Darwin, and to attend the Group's weekly seminars. Looking back at some of these emails, I am reminded of his unique email style. Rather than inefficiently polishing and refining replies, he rattled them out at the command line, without the ability to edit what he'd written so far. Brain to text, always progressing, no looking back!

He radiated infectious enthusiasm and inclusivity. There were no artificial boundaries. Social justice cross-fertilised with academic research cross-fertilised with fun. Institutional limits were irrelevant, and he preferred to explore topics from first principles and in his own style, only later checking whether what he had derived was already known in the literature.

Go to him with a problem, and you'd come away with six more to investigate. Trying to keep up was not always easy for a PhD student, but it was truly inspiring. I am honoured to have been part of his world.

Name: Dr. Saul Griffith
Tribute: David was a legend in energy and environment using reason and his powers of communication, math, and estimation, to build logical frameworks for how to deal with the energy aspect of climate change. I met David through this work.  I think we started writing books on energy at about the same time, but with his typical discipline David beat me to publication by 5 or more years with the wonderful tome "Sustainable Energy Without the Hot Air".  My book Electrify (MIT Press) focussed this work on the American context and added policy context. I only got to meet David once, in Cambridge, and we spent a delightful few days. We shared more than an interest in energy, also in information theory and folding bicycles. His guided tour of Cambridge will be a lifelong memory for me, as are many little snippets he shared.  "All human activity is folly" was a wonderful way of expressing that we shouldn't judge other people's uses and desires for use of energy. His other sage advice: an electric blanket is by far the most efficient way to sleep warm. David was instantly lovable and I miss him dearly if only to see his name pop up in my inbox again to discuss some minutiae of energy and climate.

Name: Amin Shokrollahi
Tribute: I first came to know David through his pioneering work on LDPC codes in the late 1990s. I was deeply struck by the originality of his ideas and by the unexpected connections he revealed between coding theory, physics, and machine learning. Over the years, we collaborated on problems in coding theory, and he generously served as a co-referee for one of my PhD students at EPFL. What always stayed with me was the richness of his thinking: he had a rare gift for looking at a problem from multiple angles and drawing brilliant links between seemingly distant fields. Every discussion with him left me intellectually enriched. Ten years ago, I had the honor of speaking at the MacKay conference, shortly before his untimely passing. It was there that I fully appreciated the breadth of his impact—not only as a scientist and engineer, but as a human being whose curiosity, generosity, and integrity touched so many lives. His death was a profound loss for science at large, and especially for machine learning and information theory. He remains a role model for many of us.

Name: Jade Theriault
Tribute: I love Dasher. I’m an artist and AT professional as well as a functional quadriplegic with limited hand use so the minimal clicking saves so much time. I also have ADHD and the speed and visual stimulation options are paramount to my focus. It almost feels like a gamified typing software. Best part is showing it off to my friends and colleagues for the “oos” and “ahhs.” I just know this project was developed with disabled people in mind, particularly those who are unsatisfied with most other accessible typing options. So I appreciate the work from David MacKay and whoever else is/was involved with this project.

Name: Dr Archy de Berker
How_knew_David: My girlfriend was a student of his, and recommended his book
Tribute:
David was a brilliant and brave polymath who inspired me to go to wherever the important problems were. He was willing to contribute at whatever level of technical depth was most impactful - from software to hardware to policy. I've tried to follow that example, putting on different hats and learning whatever skills were necessary to make progress towards the goal that he first articulated for me, building a decarbonized grid. 

Many brilliant academics bury their insights under layers of jargon and pomp - David was unusually able to share his clearly and simply, in a way that benefited far more people.

Name: Prof. Philipp Hennig, PhD
How_knew_David: I was the last PhD student to join the Inference Group, in 2007
Tribute: A growing chorus of algorithmically amplified pied pipers seeks to fog our minds. David, though, wasn’t just committed to the truth, he also had the rare ability to infect others with the clarity of his thoughts. He transmitted lucidity through words, drawings, and code. To receive an individualised dose of this treatment was among the greatest privileges of my life. Because David spoke not to persuade, but to empower, people enjoyed learning even difficult truths from him. As humanity considers leaving the thinking to the machines, David's absence seems all the more painful. We lost a beacon, just as night began to fall.

Name: Will Wade
How_knew_David: Collaborated on Dasher
Tribute:
I joined the Ace Centre just as the initial trials for Dasher were concluding. At the time, I was relatively new to the field, and though I had experience working with disabilities, I found myself constantly frustrated by the agonizingly slow interfaces of traditional communication systems. Seeing Dasher for the first time changed everything; I was absolutely blown away.

Over the years, I have returned to David’s videos time and again, drawn to his clarity and vision. My only regret is that I didn't have more opportunities to work with him directly. Since then, it has been my privilege to support over 50 people worldwide in using Dasher. To this day, nothing else—nothing—matches the speed and fluidity it offers to mouse and head-pointer users. Seeing users reach speeds of 32 WPM is a testament to David’s genius.

As we now seek funding for the next iteration of Dasher, incorporating modern language models and updated design, I am filled with hope. The future is bright, and while I am deeply saddened that David isn’t here to see it, I hope his family and colleagues know that his legacy is alive, thriving, and still changing lives across the globe.

Name: Anthony Heading
How_knew_David: worked in the same field,  he was a mentor
Tribute: David was extraordinary.   Inspiring, kind, wise, creative; endlessly insightful,  far ahead of me but tremendously patient and generous with his time.   I remember an afternoon in his rooms in Cambridge, one of Keith Jarrett's Sun Bear concerts playing on some fine vinyl turntable, when he solved a problem that had stumped me.    Effortlessly, and then he took the time to teach me a new subject and a whole new way of thinking.    If they say never to meet your heroes,  David was a perfect counterexample,  a fully-qualified intellectually giant in the abstract,  but then an amazing human being underneath.

Name: Steve Saling
How_knew_David: David was an online friend and mentor related to Dasher.
Tribute: I met David online about 2 years before he died. I have ALS and had become a big fan of Dasher. He introduced me to Ada Majorek and I became intimately involved with the latest release of Dasher 5.0. To say David MacKay changed my life would be an understatement. He returned my voice that ALS had so cruelly taken from me. Thank you David. You will be remembered forever. ️❤️

Name: Owen Kent
Tribute: As a person with a disability, David's work into alternative computer input has allowed me to communicate more effectively and live more independently in my community. Particularly during my college days, his software Dasher allowed me to graduate from UC Berkeley.

Name: Philip Sterne
How_knew_David: PhD student of his.
Tribute:
ITILA was the book that convinced me to apply to David’s group. It was the first text I encountered that combined deep mathematical rigor with intellectual playfulness. I remember joking that my supervisor had written an academic chapter on why sex was important — but what really struck me was his ability to treat serious ideas with both precision and curiosity. That tone shaped how I came to think about research.

It was a privilege to spend 4 years with David doing a PhD. David had a rare combination - he was intimidatingly smart, and also yet so approachable and enthusiastic. I remember someone coming to give a talk on their PhD (probably in the hopes of a postdoc). Early on in the presentation they pulled up a slide with a specific loss function that they wanted to optimize. On seeing the loss function he immediately raised his hand, and predicted all the results that were about to be presented, but then he also listed his concerns that this was the wrong loss function. An absolutely devastating critique of the talk, and yet it was also obvious that this wasn't done in a mean way, it was just really important to him to get the details right. He was a good guy to have on your side!

Late in my PhD, I would periodically email David and admit how stressed out I was. He would always give me a time to meet and discuss things even though he was super busy with his new role at the Chief Scientific Advisor to DECC. He always had kind and encouraging words for me, and I would leave with a new energy and optimism.

I won't ever have David's smarts, but since then I have always tried to emulate his patience and kindness.

Name: Sebastian Pape
How_knew_David: Through his many papers on Dasher
Tribute: He changed the life of many people around the globe through his work on Dasher, giving them a voice via a writing method build for those who could not use any other. Despite never being able to meet him before his passing, he ultimately also changed my life after I found Dasher, as it became my main research focus for my PhD in the last 6 years. Thanks David!

Name: Steph Willis
How_knew_David: Read his book and student of his
Tribute:
David shaped my whole career. As a 17 year old wondering what I might usefully do in the world I read SEWTHA and was blown away. By the clarity of the thinking, by the back of the envelope maths. I loved it. Off the back of that I decided to do an Engineering degree and focus on clean energy. 

At uni I was then lucky enough to go to a bunch of his lectures and he just continued to be a massive inspiration. In particular his explanation of why stabilising emissions wasn't enough has always stuck with me: framing the area under the curve of CO2 concentration over time as "suffering" to make clear that getting emissions to zero isn't enough - that you will eventually need some negative emissions and maybe even solar radiation management to get back to baseline. 

I now work in climate tech and try and do something useful to move us towards electrifying heating. I get all of our team to read the book and have basically bought copies of it to give to colleagues at every job I've ever done. The fact I work on climate at all, how I think about it, and how I try to communicate about it are all directly because David wrote SEWTHA. 

I'm so indebted to him and so grateful to him and so so sad that he didn't have longer to have even more impact.

Name: Dr Samuel Duffield
How_knew_David: Great admirer of his work and books
Tribute: David's approach and skill in determining and impacting valuable lines of enquiry provides an incredible example to us all. As demonstrated by his research and books which continue to provide great insight.

Name: Bastian Eppler
How_knew_David: read his book
Tribute: I learned so much from his book ITILA.

Name: Jossy Sayir
How_knew_David: we worked together at the Department of Engineering in Cambridge in 2015-2016
Tribute: Working closely with David in the last year of his life had a profound impact on my teaching and on my work. I am grateful to have had the opportunity to be part of David's life and continue to apply much of what I've learned from him on a daily basis. I could write an encyclopedia of anecdotes from my time working with David but will pick one here. After inadvertently mispronouncing David's surname during a talk I gave in December 2015, I got the following short email from him: "Oh btw, just a bit of error-correction: my name MacKay rhymes with black eye. (not pat{\’e})"

Name: Julian Allwood
Tribute: At the same time David was developing the material for SEWTHA I was leading a team looking at the options for decarbonising industry - a topic which David treats only rather lightly in his book.  We swapped ideas during the process, and following the launch of his book, he kindly put me in touch with the same publisher, and we duly followed SEWTHA with our book "Sustainable Materials: with both eyes open." Once our book was out, David was a generous advocate for us, and chaired a Royal Society public lecture I gave on it, helping to promote it.  We continued to share ideas, particularly about scalability, throughout his time as CSA in DECC.

Name: Cory Doctorow
Tribute: There's no shortage of popular *science* books, and these are quite useful if you want to satisfy your curiosity about why things are the way they are. But David pursued popular *engineering* books, and these were an invitation to imagine *how things could be*. MacKay didn't satisfy your curiosity, instead, he instilled a hunger for action, by drawing our attention to the gap between the glorious possible and the dismal now.

Name: Tim Coote
How_knew_David: Read book became collaborator in a small way
Tribute: SEWTHA was great for building arguments on sane approaches to combating climate change. I had a small interaction with David on some details in the text. I also got a lot of value from some of his work on HCI.

Name: Peter Coles
Tribute:
As I said at the time of his death:
I didn’t actually know David very well personally – we met only a few times – but on each occasion I was struck not only by his sheer intelligence, but also his energy and the force  of his personality. You meet few people who make such a lasting impression so quickly as David. He was forthright in his views, but always honest and engaging. The word “luminary” definitely applied to him. One time we met was at a meeting about Bayesian Cosmology about a decade ago. He asked a question during my talk, which triggered a lively discussion that carried on into the coffee break. I was impressed that he saw immediately how to tackle a problem that I had struggled with for months. I feel honoured to have made his acquaintance, however briefly, and can’t even begin to imagine what people who were closer to him must be feeling at his loss in such a cruel fashion. I send my deepest condolences go out to his family and friends. He was brilliant and amazing person, and will be greatly missed.

Name: Peter Dayan
How_knew_David: Colleague
Tribute: There was never a better time at the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit than 3:45pm when it was David's turn to give a talk. Perfectly crafted explanations of fascinating phenomena with hot tea, and nary a hint of hot air.

Name: Andrew Eckford
How_knew_David: Read his book and worked in related areas
Tribute: David was a professor while I was doing my Ph.D., and we happened to be working in the same area at the time: applications of statistical inference to information theory and error-correcting codes. I had the privilege of meeting him once, and I remember him being kind and gracious as I described my project to him. More generally, it was always a pleasure to read David’s work, especially his textbook. He had a unique perspective on information-theoretic work that made his work fresh and insightful, and he was clearly talented as both a scientist and a communicator.

Name: Dave Forney, Adjunct Professor Emeritus MIT EECS
Tribute: David MacKay was certainly a remarkable individual who, among a great many other things, made a huge impact on information theory and coding by his rediscovery of Gallager’s low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes and his demonstration that they could be used to approach the Shannon limit with loopy-belief-propagation decoding.  By now, LDPC codes have become the most widely used capacity-approaching codes in practice.

Name: Mike Cates FRS
How_knew_David: colleague and personal friend
Tribute:
I first got to know David on his return to Cambridge from Caltech, post PhD, initially via my younger brother Andrew. David bought a house close to mine on Thornton Road, and we frequently visited each other for meals, music and conversation. His intellectual integrity and personal generosity were apparent from the start. David introduced me to the romantic composers and many films, and I introduced him to the music of Arvo Part and to Shostakovich's 24 Preludes and Fugues. After I moved to Edinburgh in 1995 David became a regular visitor, and we went walking together in the Highlands. Our adventures included a traverse of the Aonach Eagach (the two of us, plus Matthew Bramley), which started around 4pm and ended in a nocturnal descent beside the Clachaig Gully that even David found alarming. But we were young-ish and fool-ish and the risks seemed acceptable at the time. 

A few years later (or was it earlier?) David patiently guided me to the tops of most of the Cuillins (in Skye), his scrambling skills vastly exceeding my own. This was during one of those magical summers when a high-pressure system gets stuck over the Highlands, creating unlimited sunshine and visibility for weeks at a time. Memories of that trip form a permanent highlight of my 20 years in Scotland. Sporadically throughout those years we discussed science, the energy crisis, atheism, environmentalism, vegetarianism, politics, our personal lives, and almost everything in between. 

I returned to Cambridge in mid-2015 and started seeing more of David and his family, but in less than a year he was gone. His funeral was marked by a hand-decorated cardboard coffin, a samba band, and children blowing bubbles across the grave. It was a fitting tribute to a life that, although cut short, was so purposeful and so well-lived.

Since then, the world has changed, though not for the better. During David's lifetime, fewer and fewer of our political and business leaders rejected the unambiguous warnings of science: bad choices, made now for short-term gain, risk extinguishing our collective future. Now, more and more of them not only reject the science, but gleefully embrace those bad choices, as a badge of political honour. Faced with such monumental folly, I doubt even David, were he alive today, could steer us onto a less destructive path. But I know he would try, and miss the combination of realism, optimism, energy and practical action that he would bring to the task.

Name: Dan Costello Professor Emeritus, University of Notre Dame
Tribute: David's contributions to the field of Information Theory and particularly to Coding Theory were remarkable given that his ideas had such an immediate impact on the then nascent area of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes.  The insights he brought to the construction of LDPC codes completely transformed the way researchers approached this problem, and they continue to influence the design of capacity-approaching codes to this day.  His time working in our field was far too short, but his achievements will never be forgotten.

Name: Hannah Ritchie
How_knew_David: Read his book
Tribute: David MacKay's work completely changed how I think and talk about energy. It's now my job to communicate challenges in energy, climate, environment and other topics; I do that through the lens of data, and I owe a huge part of that to David's book, SEWTHA. David had a talent for understanding the minute complexity of energy systems while being able to step back and see the bigger picture; that's what made his work so powerful, and why his legacy continues to this day. I would love it if he were still here today, not least to hear what he thought about how things have changed, and where we need to go next. I never spoke to David personally, but I owe him a lot. He is missed.

Name: Coryn Bailer-Jones
How_knew_David: I was his postdoc from 1997-1998 at the Cavnedish
Tribute: I learned an awful lot from David during my 1.5 year postdoc with him (1997-1998). He was full of ideas and energy, was widely interested (I remember one heated lunchtime discussion about the likely intelligence of stone age people), opinionated (aren’t all Bayesians?), sometimes impatient, but passionate about both teaching and learning. His group was working on a wide range of cutting edge problems, and I learned a lot from the extended discussions in our group meetings and our numerous visitors. I count David as one of a handful of deeply inspiring people I have had the fortune to interact with in my life.

Name: Mike Pickles
How_knew_David: He was a visiting lecturer at the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences (AIMS) when I was resident lecturer there 2003-6.
Tribute: I met David when he was teaching at AIMS. He was of course a brilliant man and a dedicated teacher, but what I particularly remember him for is an act of kindness. During my second year at AIMS, there had been some internal conflicts about the institute's direction that caused the loss of some of the leadership. The task of supporting students and ensuring continuity in the course largely fell to me, at the time a recent postdoc. David came and offered to move to AIMS full-time to help, an insanely generous offer which would have uprooted his whole life, but that conversation really helped me, both because of the offer itself and just the act of checking up to support someone more junior. David has been one of my role models, both as a researcher and a teacher.

Name: Rt Hon Ed Miliband MP, Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero
Tribute: It was my privilege to work with Professor David MacKay when I was Secretary of State for Energy and Climate Change and he served as our first Chief Scientific Adviser. I will always remember his ability to think big, explain the complex in simple terms, and his passion for his subject. He is deeply missed for his wisdom, intelligence, values and humanity.

Name: Jonny Edwards
How_knew_David: read both books, and had some brief communications.
Tribute: It's not so much the books or the outputs (although they are all genuinely astounding), it's more the person. For me David held the torch for genuine interest and excitement in new ideas, and had the real power to explain and innovate. He absolutely changed my professional life in so many ways, I ultimately started a business because he was very complementary about an idea I had. All I can say is I will try to pass on his enthusiasm and keep my own "beginners mind". Love and Thanks.

Name: (anonymous)
How_knew_David: Student of his
Tribute: David was always so clear and so right.  ITILA remains a point of reference despite how much the AI revolution has moved the field on since its publication over 20 years ago.  Many people in Cambridge and beyond have advanced their knowledge and understanding through its clear exposition of a diverse set of topics.

Name: Neil Gershenfeld
How_knew_David: lots of mutual contacts
Tribute: David had a tremendous impact on my approach to mathematical modeling, through his uncanny ability to think simultaneously creatively and critically.

Name: Professor Per Ola Kristensson
How_knew_David: Postdoctoral Advisor
Tribute: David was my postdoctoral advisor at the Inference Group in the Cavendish Laboratory when I was a Junior Resarch Fellow. I first met David in a workshop in Glasgow where someone in the audience kept interrupting my talk with a lot of questions. We spoke afterwards and I realised that spending time in his research group would be an eye opener. Before I met David I did not belive geniuses truly exist. You hear about some of them in the abstract but you tend not to encounter them in real life. David was a true genius. It is fascinating how his mind worked and how generous he was with his time, ideas, and intellect. David's books fully encompass the same ethos. They are about someone wanting you to truly understanding topics of great importance. The empathy to the student and the reader is always present. I feel very privileged having worked with David during those foundational years, which very much made me a different and better researcher and educator. I remember him sitting in his office working on his new book 'Without the Hot Air' until 1am in the Cavendish Laboratory. The wide range of intellectual contributions and the dedication to not just research or education but society at large is worth celebrating as an example of just how much it is possible to achieve in such a tragically short lifespan.

Name: Neil Kermode
How_knew_David: Read his book
Tribute:
SEWTHA was a breath of fresh air through the stuffy siloed booths of people bickering about irrelevancies of energy production and use. Of course we need to be efficient in our use of energy, but that might be better achieved by not buying the latest phone rather than making sure you get a new one with some 'eco' setting and unplugging the charger.

My greatest regret is that when he came up to Orkney to see the pioneering work on marine energy and general renewables work that I missed him. I was probably away from Orkney bickering with someone over the latest piece of governmental lunacy and missed his talk in the Royal Hotel. I always planned to get to see him in person another time...

Name: Alexander James Phillips
How_knew_David: Read his book and exchanged some emails on UK energy.
Tribute: Looking back on his book and on our email exchanges, albeit too few, I realise now how huge an inspiration his approach was for my life trajectory.  I was equally bemused by the hot air of confusing conversation, so much so I quit my PhD in biotech at Cambridge to try to build some kind of new medium for collective sense making.  Fast forward 15 years and I'm still trying, but getting a lot closer now, and again I find myself returning to his work to act as another foundational pillar and guide in that journey.

Name: Prof. Andrew Gelman
Tribute:
In his classic 2003 book on information theory, David wrote that, "in many problems, we really only need about twelve independent samples."  He explains:  "Now, how accurately would a manager like to know [a parameter] Φ? I would suggest there is little point in knowing Φ to a precision finer than about σ/3. After all, the true cost is likely to differ by ±σ from Φ. If we obtain R = 12 independent samples from P(x), we can estimate Φ to a precision of σ/√12 – which is smaller than σ/3. So twelve samples suffice."

This led me to wonder . . .  . . . where did the “12” come from in MacKay’s passage?  When I first saw the number there, I assumed it would have something to do with the variance of the uniform distribution. But that doesn’t seem to come up at all.  Accepting MacKay’s stipulation that σ/3 would be enough precision in this sort of example, shouldn’t he have said that 9 random draws would suffice?  I could see him rounding that up to 10.  Or even 16, if he wanted to get all base-2 on us.  But why 12?  I didn't get this at all.

So I asked David.  Here was his reply:  "You said that can imagine rounding up 9 to 10 – which would be elegant if we worked in base 10.  But in the UK we haven’t switched to base 10 yet, we still work in dozens and grosses. . . . Probably in an earlier draft of the book in 2001 I said 'a dozen', rather than '12'. Then some feedbacker may have written and said 'I don’t know what a dozen is'; so then I sacrificed elegant language and replaced “dozen” by '12', which leads to your mystification."

This reminds me that, when I was a kid, my dad told me that in Britain there was a Duodecimal Society, devoted to promoting base 12.  This was told to me in a "There will always be an England" sort of thing.  In writing this note, I was curious so I looked it up on the web, and it turns out that there is such a society, but it was first established in the United States.  So there!  I guess David was more American than he realized.

Name: Carl Edward Rasmussen
How_knew_David: colleague and friend
Tribute:
Tribute to David J C MacKay by Carl Edward Rasmussen

David was probably the person who influenced my thinking most, apart from my immediate supervisors. He was always kind, very generous with his time, and a clear and inspirational thinker. Our trajectories were surprisingly interwoven.

I first met David in Edinburgh in 1991. I was an engineering student at the Technical University of Denmark on a year long visit at the Centre for Cognitive Science in Edinburgh, and David was a PhD student at Caltech, visiting Edinburgh and giving a talk. His talk was on his thesis research on Bayesian inference in neural networks. This was a topic which I had never heard about at the time. And David's talk blew me away, I still remember it clearly. David's enthusiasm and clear explanations were extremely contagious. This one encounter greatly influenced my scientific trajectory. After returning to Copenhagen I wrote my MSc thesis on comparing David's evidence framework with the competing regularisation framework for training of neural networks.

During my thesis work I ran into some conceptual difficulties which had to do with certain mathematical limits governing inference. I had access to email, which was probably a bit unusual for students at the time. So I emailed David to ask for advice. Within a day I had an elaborate reply with calculations, explanations and plots, which helped me tremendously. I later discovered that it was typical of David to be so generous with his time. He thought it the most natural thing to help a stuck student who he didn't know.

When I joined Geoff Hinton's neural network group in Toronto, I found that David visited for a few weeks every summer. These were exciting times. I worked on Gaussian Processes, directly inspired by Bayesian inference in neural networks. David continued his work on Bayesian inference and worked on error correcting codes. His work on low density parity check codes clarified that these codes are able to reach the Shannon channel capacity limit, a fundamental result which wasn't widely known before David's work.

After my PhD I was a post doc at the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit at UCL in London, where David had a part time contract. During this time I visited David's group in Cambridge and Darwin College multiple times, which was always very exciting and covering a wide range of topics.

David was a gifted lecturer. In his information theory course he would construct and analyse an error correcting code based on suggestions from the audience, an audacious and inspiring display of thinking on the fly. He was also demanding of his audience; once he jumped on the desk in the lecture hall, complaining that the audience wasn't interactive enough, "this doesn't work for me!"

David's exceedingly high standards didn't always make it easy for collaborators.
